reference.source: GeneReviews / Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: A neurodevelopmental disorder caused by heterozygous loss-of-function variants in HNRNPK
Developmental delay and intellectual disability accompany marked infantile hypotonia
A distinctive facial appearance includes downturned corners of the mouth, ptosis, and a long palpebral fissure aperture
Congenital heart defects and genitourinary anomalies, including renal malformation, are frequently present
Skeletal features such as craniosynostosis and connective tissue laxity may occur
Feeding difficulties and, in some, structural brain anomalies are reported
Most cases are de novo, arising as new dominant variants rather than being inherited
Diagnosis is established by identifying an HNRNPK variant, usually through exome or panel testing
reference.pathophysiology: Au-Kline syndrome is caused by heterozygous loss-of-function variants in HNRNPK, which encodes a heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein that binds nucleic acids and participates in the regulation of transcription, RNA splicing, messenger RNA stability, and translation. Through these activities HNRNPK influences the expression of many genes during development, and reducing its dosage disrupts the coordinated developmental programmes of the brain, heart, kidneys, and skeleton. The resulting haploinsufficiency produces the intellectual disability, hypotonia, characteristic facial features, and the cardiac, renal, and skeletal anomalies of the syndrome. The condition is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner and typically arises de novo.
additionalDifferentials: Kabuki syndrome, with overlapping facial and developmental features

additionalInvestigations: Exome or gene panel testing to identify an HNRNPK variant
Craniofacial imaging to assess for craniosynostosis
Developmental assessment and neuroimaging where indicated
Feeding and growth evaluation in infancy
redFlags: Feeding failure with aspiration and faltering growth
reference.prognosis: Lifespan is generally not markedly shortened, and the outlook is dominated by intellectual disability of variable degree together with the management of any cardiac, renal, and skeletal anomalies; developmental progress is expected with support, and the presence and severity of major structural anomalies principally shape the long-term outcome.
pitfalls: Mislabelling the child as Kabuki syndrome and not pursuing HNRNPK testing
Overlooking craniosynostosis and its risk of raised intracranial pressure
Failing to screen for cardiac and renal anomalies at diagnosis
Assuming inheritance from a parent when most cases are de novo
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
management: No disease-specific drug therapy; management centres on early developmental intervention with physiotherapy, occupational and speech and language therapy for hypotonia and developmental delay
Echocardiographic assessment and cardiology management of congenital heart defects
Renal tract imaging with nephrology and urology follow-up for genitourinary and renal malformations
Craniofacial and neurosurgical assessment with surgical correction of craniosynostosis where present
Feeding and nutritional support in infancy, including nasogastric or gastrostomy feeding for feeding difficulties
Surveillance of growth, vision and hearing, with neuroimaging for structural brain anomalies as indicated
Genetic counselling for the family; the condition is autosomal dominant and usually arises de novo
Multidisciplinary coordination across clinical genetics, paediatrics, cardiology and developmental services
